readings.c3s1:
{{smaller|several different trouts (not chars) of the western parts of North America, of the genus ''Salmo''. See def. 1 (''b'').—'''Brown trout''', the common European trout, ''Salmo fario''.—'''Californian brook-trout''', the rainbow-trout, ''Salmo irideus''. See cut under ''rainbow-trout''.—'''Cutthroat trout''', the Rocky Mountain brook-trout.—'''Deep-water trout.''' (''a'') The great lake-trout. [Great Lakes.] (''b'') A weakfish or sea-trout, ''Cynoscion thalassinus''. [Charleston, U.S.]—'''Dolly Varden trout''', a Californian char, ''Salvelinus malma''.—'''Galway trout''', ''Salmo gallivensis'' of England.—'''Gillaroo trout''', ''Salmo stomachicus'' of England.—'''Golden trout''', the rainbow-trout.—'''Gray trout''', a sea-trout—the squeteague. See cut under ''weakfish''.—'''Great lake-trout.''' (''a'') ''Salvelinus namaycush''. See def. 2. (''b'') ''Salmo ferox'' of England.—'''Ground-trout''', a malformed common trout (''Salmo fario'') of Penygant in Yorkshire, England, having a singular protrusion of the under jaw.—'''Lake Tahoe trout''', a variety of ''Salmo purpuratus'' found in Lake Tahoe, Pyramid Lake, and streams of the Sierra Nevada. Also called locally ''silver trout'' and ''black trout''.—'''Loch Leven trout''', ''Salmo levenensis'' of Great Britain.—'''Loch Stennis trout''', ''Salmo orcadensis'' of Great Britain.—'''Mackinaw trout''', the great lake-trout. See cut under ''lake-trout'', 2.—'''Malma trout''', the Dolly Varden trout.—'''Mountain-trout.''' (''a'') The black-spotted trout. (''b'') The black-bass, ''Micropterus salmoides''. [Local, U. S.]—'''Ocean trout.''' See ''ocean''.—'''Pot-bellied trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Red-spotted trout.''' (''a'') Same as ''brook-trout'' (''a''). (''b'') The Dolly Varden trout.—'''Red trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Reef-trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Rio Grande trout''', ''Salmo spilurus'', inhabiting also the streams of the Utah basin.—'''River-trout''', the common European trout, ''Salmo fario''.—'''Rocky Mountain brook-trout''', ''Salmo purpuratus'', the Yellowstone trout, or salmon-trout of the Columbia river. See cut under ''Salmo''.—'''St. Mary’s trout''', the three-bearded rockling. [Local, British (Penryn).]—'''Salt-water trout''', a sea-trout—the squeteague, or a related species of ''Cynoscion''. See ''Cynoscion'', and cut under ''weakfish''.—'''Schoodic trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Sebago trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Shad-trout''', the trout-shad or squeteague.—'''Shoal-water trout''', the great lake-trout.—'''Silver trout.''' (''a'') A malformed common trout (''S. fario'') of Malham Tarn in Yorkshire, England, having a defective gill-cover. (''b'') The black-spotted trout, or mountain-trout of western North America. (''c'') The Lake Tahoe trout.—'''Speckled trout''', the brook-trout.—'''Spotted trout.''' (''a'') One of different American trouts spotted (1) with black (see def. 1 (''b'')); (2) with red—a speckled trout (see def. 2). (''b'') The weakfish or sea-trout ''Cynoscion maculatus''.—'''Sun-trout''', the squeteague, ''Cynoscion regalis''.—'''Waha Lake trout''', a local variety of ''Salmo purpuratus'', found in Waha Lake, Washington.—'''White trout.''' (''a'') A variety of ''Salmo fario''. See ''finnac''. (''b'') The bastard trout.—'''Yellowstone trout''', ''Salmo purpuratus'', the Rocky Mountain brook-trout. See cut under ''Salmo''.—'''Yellow trout''', a malformed trout with the same defect as the silver trout (''a''). (See also ''bull trout'', ''lake-trout'', ''rainbow-trout'', ''rock trout'', ''salmon-trout'', ''sea-trout''.)}}

'''trough''' (trôf), ''v.'' [< ''trough'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To feed grossly, as a hog from a trough. ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, VIII. 168.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make into a trough, or into the shape of a trough. ''Proc. Soc. Psychical Research'', III. 461.

'''trough-battery''' (trôf′bat″ėr-i), ''n.'' A form of voltaic battery in which the glass or porcelain cells are replaced by a trough of wood or other insulating material divided into sections by insulating plates. {{smaller|Cruikshank’s trough-battery consists of a trough of baked wood divided into cells by metallic partitions consisting of a plate of zinc and a plate o copper soldered back to back.}}

'''trough-fault''' (trôf′fâlt), ''n.'' In ''geol.'', two faults having nearly the same direction, but dipping toward each other, so that the mass of rock included between them has more or less of th form of a wedge. {{smaller|The fault-block in such cases is tr angular in cross-section, instead of being rectangular, a it would be if the faults both had the same dip.}}

'''trough-gutter''' (trôf′gut″ėr), ''n.'' A trough-shape gutter below the eaves of buildings.

'''trough-room''' (trôf′röm), ''n.'' In ''fish-culture'', hatching-house.

'''trough-shell''' (trôf′shel), ''n.'' A round clam; member of the ''Mactridæ'' (where see cut), esp cially the British ''Mactra solida'' and ''M. st torum''. {{smaller|These have a shell of nearly triangular fo with thick opaque valves covered with brownish epid mis; a V-shaped cardinal tooth is in one valve, wit long lateral tooth on each side, fitting into deep groo of the opposite valve. Both species live buried in sand near low-water mark. In some places they are teemed for the table, and in the Netherlands the shells much used for making roads and paths.}}

'''troul†''' (trōl), ''v.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''tro''

'''trounce''' (trouns), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''troun'' ppr. ''trouncing''. [Early mod. E. ''trounse''; < ''troncer'', cut, mutilate, = Sp. ''tronzar'', shatte OF. ''tronce'', a piece of timber, ''tronche'', a g piece of timber, a stump; cf. OF. ''tronc'', tru cf. also ''tronçon'', ''tronson'', a truncheon; < L. ''t'' ''cus'', a trunk: see ''trunk'' and ''truncheon''.] punish or beat severely; thrash or whip sm ly; castigate. [Now colloq.]
{{smaller block|The Lord ''trounsed'' [discomfited, R. V.] Sisara and a charettes.
{{right|''Bible of'' 1551, Judges}}
<poem>Well, sir, you’ll dearly answer this:
My master’s constable; he’ll ''trounce'' you for ’t.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'' (?), Faithful Friend}}}}

'''troupe''' (tröp), ''n.'' [< F. ''troupe'', a troop, a pany: see ''troop''.] A troop; a company; ticularly, a company of players, operatic formers, dancers, acrobats, etc.

{{smaller block|She showed me a ''troupe'' of faire ladies, every o lover colling and kissing, chinning and embracing
{{right|''Breton'', Dreame of Strange Effect}}}}

'''troupial,''' ''n.'' See ''troopial.''

'''trous-de-loup''' (trö′dė-lö′), ''n. pl.'' [F.: pl. of ''trou'', hole; ''de'', of; ''loup'' (< L. ''l'' wolf: see ''wolf''.] Trap-holes or pits dug ground, in the form of inverted cones o mids, each with a pointed stake in th dle, to serve as obstacles to an enemy.

'''trouse†''' (trouz), ''n.'' [Also ''trews'', q. v.; ''trousse'': see ''trousers'', ''truss''.] Trousers;

{{smaller block|[Ventidius] served as a footman in his single ''tr''
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pli}} grieues.}}

'''troused†''' (trouzd), ''a.'' [< ''trouse'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] I ing trousers; clothed with trousers. I Polyolbion, xxii. Also ''trowsed.''

'''trousering''' (trou′zėr-ing), ''n.'' [< ''tro'' ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] Cloth for making trousers, es material made for the purpose.

'''trousers''' (trou′zėrz), ''n. pl.'' [Formerly a ''sers, trowzers, trossers;'' a later form, wit accidental intrusion of ''r'', of ''trouses, trou'' ''trooze, trews''), < OF. ''trousses'', pl., tru breeches, pl. of ''trousse'', bundle, pack ''truss'', of which ''trousers'' is thus ult. a tiated plural.] A garment for men, e from the waist to the ankles, covering part of the trunk and each leg separate nally, tightly fitting drawers; pantalo ''strossers.'' {{smaller|In the early part of the ninetee long frilled drawers reaching to the ankles w girls and women, and called ''trousers.''}}
{{smaller block|The youth and people of fashion, when in wear ''trowsers'', with shoes and stockings.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the E}}

''Trousers'' (braccæ) were not worn till after and Celtic wars, and even then only by soldi exposed to northern climates. {{right|''Encyc.'' E}}

On the abandonment of the latter [bases breeches or sloppes became an important part of apparell; and while the long hose we}} {{RunningHeader||6503|}}
{{smaller block|planted by or new christened the ''trauses'' [read ''trouses''], the upper stock or the breeches worn over them received the name of trunk hose.
{{right|''Planché.''}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Breeches, Trousers, Pantaloons.'' ''Breeches'' are properly short clothes, reaching just below the knee; the use of the word for ''trousers'' is erroneous and vulgar. ''Trousers'' is the old word for the garment common in Occidental nations to cover the legs of men; many, especially in England, still insist upon the word.and confine ''pantaloons'' to its historical sense. Many, however, especially in America, are satisfied with ''pantaloons'' (colloquially, ''pants'') for ''trousers''}}.

'''trousse''' (trös), ''n.'' [F., a bundle, quiver: see ''truss.''] A number of small utensils carried in a case or sheath together; especially, such a sheath with knives, tweezers, and the like, hung from the girdle, and worn during the middle ages. Compare ''étui'', ''equipage''<sup>1</sup>, 4. {{smaller|The trousse is now rather a collection of tools or implements for serious work, and for men rather than for women: as, a surgeon’s ''trousse''.}} {{img float|file=century v08 p0307 c2f1.png|width=60px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Trousse, from a French lumination of 1350. ''a'', t trousse. (From Viollet-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobil français.”)}}}}

'''trousseau''' (trö-sō′), ''n.''; pl. ''trousseaux'' (-sōz′). [< F. ''trousseau'', a bundle, kit, bride’s outfit, trousseau, OF. ''trousseau'', ''torsea'' a little truss or bundle (cf. It. '''trout<sup>1</sup>''' (trout), ''v. i.'' [< ''trout<sup>1</sup>'', ''n.''] To fish for or catch trout.

'''trout<sup>2</sup>†''' (trout), ''v. i.'' [Var. of ''troat.''] Same as ''troat.''
{{smaller block|''Rere.'' To bellow as a Stag, to ''trout'' as a Buck. ''Rér.'' To bellow, to bray (in tearmes of hunting we say that the red deere bells, and the fallow troytes or croynes). {{right|''Cotgrave.''}}}}

'''trout-basket''' (trout′bȧs″ket), ''n.'' An anglers’ creel for carrying trout. {{smaller|It is usually made of willow or osier, and of a size capable of containing from ten to twenty pounds of fish.}}

'''trout-bird''' (trout′bėrd), ''n.'' The American golden plover, ''Charadrius dominicus. H. P. Ives.'' [Massachusetts.]

'''trout-colored''' (trout′kul″o̤rd), ''a.'' Speckled like a trout: specifically noting a white horse spotted with black, bay, or sorrel.

'''trout-farm''' (trout′färm), ''n.'' A place where trout are bred and reared artificially.

'''troutful''' (trout′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''trout'' + ''-ful.''] Abounding in trout. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Clear and fresh rivulets of ''troutful'' water. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, II. 1.}}}}

'''trout-hole''' (trout′hōl), ''n.'' A sheltered or retired place in which trout lie.

'''trout-hook''' (trout′hu̇k), ''n.'' A fish-hook specially designed or used for catching trout.

'''troutless''' (trout′les), ''a.'' [< ''trout'' + ''-less.''] Without trout. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I catch a trout now and then, . . . so I am not left ''trout-'' {{right|''Kingsley'', Life, xxiii.}}}} ''less.''

'''troutlet''' (trout′let), ''n.'' [< ''trout'' + ''-let.''] A young or small trout; a troutling. ''Hood'', Dream of Eugene Aram.

'''trout-line''' (trout′līn), ''n.'' A fishing-line specially designed for or used in fishing for trout.

'''troutling''' (trout′ling), ''n.'' [< ''trout'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] A troutlet.

'''trout-louse''' (trout′lous), ''n.'' Same as ''sug.''

'''trout-net''' (trout′net), ''n.'' The landing-net used by anglers for removing trout from the water.

'''trout-perch''' (trout′pėrch), ''n.'' '''1.''' A fish, ''Percopsis guttatus'', of the family ''Percopsidæ''. See cut under ''Percopsis.''—'''2.''' The black-bass. [South Carolina.]

'''trout-pickerel''' (trout′pik″ėr-el), ''n.'' See ''pickerel.''

'''trout-rod''' (trout′rod), ''n.'' A fishing-rod specially adapted for taking trout.

'''trout-shad''' (trout′shad), ''n.'' The squeteague.

'''trout-spoon''' (trout′spön), ''n.'' A small revolving spoon used as an artificial bait or lure for trout.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
